questions.q: Umar ibn al-Khattab called the person who points out his shortcomings a giver of a “gift.” Why?
options: Because critics are always right
Not quite. The article says: A weakness one is unaware of cannot be corrected, so whoever reveals it is helping one grow.
Because gifts were customary among leaders
Not quite. The article says: A weakness one is unaware of cannot be corrected, so whoever reveals it is helping one grow.
Because criticism is pleasant to hear
Not quite. The article says: A weakness one is unaware of cannot be corrected, so whoever reveals it is helping one grow.
A weakness one is unaware of cannot be corrected, so whoever reveals it is helping one grow
Yes. Criticism is a mirror, not an insult.
questions.rationale: “A weakness of which you are unaware cannot be corrected. The person who makes you aware of it is, therefore, helping you in your self-development.”

questions.q: What question does a sincere seeker of truth ask about a criticism?
options: “Who has said this?”
Not quite. The article says: “Is what has been said true?” – not “Who has said this?”.
“How can I reply sharply?”
Not quite. The article says: “Is what has been said true?” – not “Who has said this?”.
“Who else heard it?”
Not quite. The article says: “Is what has been said true?” – not “Who has said this?”.
“Is what has been said true?” – not “Who has said this?”
Right. If true, he accepts it; if not, he answers calmly.
questions.rationale: “A sincere seeker of truth does not ask, ‘Who has said this?’ He asks, ‘Is what has been said true?’”

questions.q: The fan began to turn again after a hot spell without electricity. What did this ordinary event suggest to the writer?
options: That summers are growing hotter
Not quite. The article says: For a believer who lives with patience, death may be such a sudden passing from discomfort to comfort.
For a believer who lives with patience, death may be such a sudden passing from discomfort to comfort
Yes. A material event became a spiritual experience.
That power cuts should be reported
Not quite. The article says: For a believer who lives with patience, death may be such a sudden passing from discomfort to comfort.
That comfort is all that matters
Not quite. The article says: For a believer who lives with patience, death may be such a sudden passing from discomfort to comfort.
questions.rationale: “The change may be like the sudden return of electricity after a long period of oppressive heat—a transition from discomfort to unimaginable comfort.”

questions.q: Asked for proof of God, a Sufi answered, “The leaves of a tree.” What was his reasoning?
options: Leaves are too many to count
Not quite. The article says: The same soil, water and sunlight yield utterly different plants and fruits – pointing to a designed system behind them.
Leaves fall every year
Not quite. The article says: The same soil, water and sunlight yield utterly different plants and fruits – pointing to a designed system behind them.
The same soil, water and sunlight yield utterly different plants and fruits – pointing to a designed system behind them
Well read. From creation to the Creator.
Trees are older than people
Not quite. The article says: The same soil, water and sunlight yield utterly different plants and fruits – pointing to a designed system behind them.
questions.rationale: “Leaves and fruits grow from the same earth. They receive the same water and the same sunlight. Yet their results are astonishingly different.”

questions.q: How does the article distinguish ma‘rifah (realization of God) from simply knowing about God?
options: It is skill in debate
Not quite. The article says: It is a living discovery that moves the person, not mere information or argument.
It is a title given by scholars
Not quite. The article says: It is a living discovery that moves the person, not mere information or argument.
It is a larger store of facts
Not quite. The article says: It is a living discovery that moves the person, not mere information or argument.
It is a living discovery that moves the person, not mere information or argument
Correct. A flower opening can bring it about.
questions.rationale: “Ma‘rifah is not simply possessing information about God. It is a living discovery of God.”

questions.q: The article likens this life and the Hereafter to a farmer’s two seasons. Which is which?
options: Neither has any connection with the other
Not quite. The article says: This life is the season of sowing; the Hereafter is the season of harvest.
This life is the season of sowing; the Hereafter is the season of harvest
Yes. After death there is no more sowing.
This life is the harvest; the Hereafter is for sowing
Not quite. The article says: This life is the season of sowing; the Hereafter is the season of harvest.
Both are seasons of harvest
Not quite. The article says: This life is the season of sowing; the Hereafter is the season of harvest.
questions.rationale: “Our worldly life is the season of sowing; the Hereafter is the season of harvest.”

questions.q: Why does the article say the first victim of an angry reaction is oneself?
options: Because others stop listening
Not quite. The article says: Anger destroys one’s own peace and judgement, and replaying the incident repeats the harm many times.
Anger destroys one’s own peace and judgement, and replaying the incident repeats the harm many times
Right. “Save yourself.”
Because the other person always strikes back
Not quite. The article says: Anger destroys one’s own peace and judgement, and replaying the incident repeats the harm many times.
Because anger is punished by law
Not quite. The article says: Anger destroys one’s own peace and judgement, and replaying the incident repeats the harm many times.
questions.rationale: “He harmed you once; by repeatedly remembering the incident, you harm yourself many times.”

questions.q: Opponents mocked the Prophet with the name “Mudhammam.” What principle does the article draw from his reply that they were abusing Mudhammam, “while I am Muhammad”?
options: Always answer mockery with wit
Not quite. The article says: Do not take every negative remark personally – an insult becomes a quarrel only when it finds a willing participant.
Change one’s name when insulted
Not quite. The article says: Do not take every negative remark personally – an insult becomes a quarrel only when it finds a willing participant.
Insults should be reported to the elders
Not quite. The article says: Do not take every negative remark personally – an insult becomes a quarrel only when it finds a willing participant.
Do not take every negative remark personally – an insult becomes a quarrel only when it finds a willing participant
Yes. He deprived the insult of its power.
questions.rationale: “It demonstrated a profound principle of life: do not personalize every negative remark… An insult becomes a quarrel only when it finds a willing participant.”

questions.q: In the Chinese story, what was the old man’s answer to those who laughed at his plan to dig away two mountains?
options: That he would move house if he failed
Not quite. The article says: The mountains cannot grow, but with each day’s digging – by him, his sons and theirs – they must grow smaller.
That the mountains were smaller than they looked
Not quite. The article says: The mountains cannot grow, but with each day’s digging – by him, his sons and theirs – they must grow smaller.
That he would hire many workers
Not quite. The article says: The mountains cannot grow, but with each day’s digging – by him, his sons and theirs – they must grow smaller.
The mountains cannot grow, but with each day’s digging – by him, his sons and theirs – they must grow smaller
Exactly. A problem has limits; perseverance need have none.
questions.rationale: “The mountains cannot grow any bigger, while with every day’s digging they will become a little smaller. If we continue, one day they must disappear.”

questions.q: When, according to the article, is a person’s real character most clearly seen?
options: In great decisions only
Not quite. The article says: In small moments – when there is nothing to gain, no one watching and no fear of being judged.
In public speeches
Not quite. The article says: In small moments – when there is nothing to gain, no one watching and no fear of being judged.
In what others say about him
Not quite. The article says: In small moments – when there is nothing to gain, no one watching and no fear of being judged.
In small moments – when there is nothing to gain, no one watching and no fear of being judged
Well reasoned. And character can be reformed by self-examination.
questions.rationale: “It becomes especially visible when there is no advantage in doing good, no audience to appreciate us and no fear of being judged.”
